rh-l2q1-d1e6080.summary: Reply to the ninth: God co-acted with the devil's tempting of Christ by good pleasure, but the devil acted for evil viciously and unjustly, God for good justly.
claims: God and the devil concurred in Christ's temptation, justly and unjustly.

rh-l2q1-d1e6093.summary: Reply to the tenth: the same as for others' sins. God preordained Paul's sins to be an occasion of good but never commanded or counseled them, so Paul sinned without acting against God's good pleasure. All this is said for exercise without assertion. Example: a master commands Socrates to pull a ship and forbids Plato; both pull, two partial causes of one act, one justly and one unjustly. So God justly co-acts with tyrant or devil.
claims: One act can be done justly by one partial cause and unjustly by another.
These positions are offered for exercise without assertion.

rh-l2q1-d1e6135.summary: Reply to the fifth principal argument: the inference fails, since one judge may lawfully omit what pertains to another. In the relevant sense the antecedent is denied. God justly permits evils, forbidding them by laws and teaching but not violently impeding free nature in adults, and justly damns unbaptized infants for original sin. The Decretum concerns judges under law, not God, whose will is law and whatever he wills is just.
claims: God justly permits evils without violently impeding freedom.
God's will is law and whatever he wills is just.
Canon law on judges does not apply to God.

rh-l2q1-d1e6224.summary: Reply to the second form: punishment is condign either as great as the fault, as the sinner merited, or as much as it pleases the just judge to inflict. In the first sense God punishes below condign, in the second not.
claims: Condign punishment is either proportional to fault or what the judge wills.

rh-l2q1-d1e6246.summary: Objection: then any punishment could be condign for any fault, and giving Nero Judas's punishment would be condign for both, so Nero is now punished less.
claims: If condignity is what God wills, any penalty fits any fault.

rh-l2q1-d1e6259.summary: Reply: every punishment is condign in the second sense, as much as God pleases, and a lesser punishment is not therefore diminished, since being willed by him it is just and condign.
claims: Whatever punishment God wills is just and condign.

rh-l2q1-d1e6276.summary: On Anselm's 'to order sin rightly is to punish it': literally false of satisfactory punishment, since God leaves many sins unpunished for a time, awaiting repentance, without leaving disorder. To order sin is to establish penal laws and execute them opportunely, when God pleases.
claims: Ordering sin means establishing and executing penal laws when God pleases.

rh-l2q1-d1e6300.summary: On 'satisfaction must match the measure of sin': sin is measured by the law transgressed and satisfaction by the penal law. One satisfies God by undergoing the penalty he pleases to inflict, so any penalty he wills is condign satisfaction. Anselm and the saints speak after the manner of known human judgment, not all properly of the divine judge.
claims: Satisfaction is whatever penalty God wills to accept.
Anselm speaks on the model of human judgment.

rh-l2q1-d1e6332.summary: Reply to the third: grants many things go unpunished, but they are well ordered without punishment, since as God pleases so it happens justly. People wonder because they think God bound to rule by their own heads, which would go badly; when he waits he waits mercifully, when he punishes he punishes justly, and when he remits he remits mercifully and justly.
claims: Unpunished sins are not disorder, since God's pleasure orders them.
God is not bound to rule by human expectations.

rh-l2q1-d1e6356.summary: Reply to the fourth: grants each punishment is infinitely distant from the other, but denies that commuting eternal to temporal punishment is as unjust as the reverse.
claims: Commuting eternal to temporal punishment is not unjust.

rh-l2q1-d1e6372.summary: Reply to the fifth: a just judge commands only what he wills permissively. If God commanded and then impeded fulfillment without their fault, he would act unjustly. But some make themselves unfit to execute a precept, and the precept stands though God does not will its execution then, like a servant who gets drunk and cannot serve: the duty remains though the master does not want his service then.
claims: A precept remains binding when the subject makes himself unable to fulfill it.

rh-l2q1-d1e6407.summary: On Abraham and the healed man, which seem false signs since God commanded what he did not will: some say Abraham only seemed commanded. Holcot says God commanded him to sacrifice his son and did not will it, as the outcome showed.
claims: God commanded Abraham's sacrifice without willing it.

rh-l2q1-d1e6424.summary: Objection: feigning, commanding one thing and willing the opposite, is making a false sign. Reply: it does not conflict with God's justice or wisdom to feign, to signify that he wills something he does not, when it profits the one signified to, as it profited Abraham.
claims: God may feign by signifying a will he does not have, for the recipient's benefit.

rh-l2q1-d1e6453.summary: Objection: then he deceived Abraham. Granted, for Abraham's benefit. Or Abraham deceived himself, understanding the command otherwise: 'do this' and 'I will you to do this' differ, and the command meant 'I will you to act as if I willed you to sacrifice'. As for the healed blind man, Christ did not command silence literally but taught him not to seek vainglory, which he could understand from circumstances.
claims: God may beneficially deceive, or the recipient may misread the command.
A command does not signify the same as 'I will that you do this'.
Christ's injunction to silence forbade vainglory.

rh-l2q1-d1e6510.summary: Reply to the sixth principal argument: God gives the blessed more than they merited, so does them no injustice; they did not merit their joy absolutely and at once, but when God pleases. The delay does not burden them, since they will what God pleases, and needs no compensation, having been rewarded infinitely beyond what they could merit.
claims: The blessed are not wronged by delay, having received more than they merited.

rh-l2q1-d1e6543.summary: Reply to the seventh: grants God requires justice of the reprobate by precept but does not will it by good pleasure, since they do not will it.
claims: God requires by precept what he does not will by good pleasure from the reprobate.

rh-l2q1-d1e6552.summary: Reply to the argument about remission to two damned: God remits less in quantity to one but an equal proportion, a half or third or whatever he pleases, so neither is wronged and each receives proportioned mercy. This ends the question.
claims: God remits equal proportions of punishment to the damned.
